segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was the word for "with" in Spanish, and we have it in words like "convenient", "conform"...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So con is "with", and we have it as like a Latin building block in many Latin-English words. Consequence: with sequence.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, in Spanish, you don't say "with her", "with him", "with them", you actually just say "with he", "with she", "with they". So, how would you say "with him" or "with he"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I mean if it was feminine group?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nos is "us", but of course in Spanish we won't say "with us", we will say "with we".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, con nosotros. What if you were an all-female group?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Con nosotras, good. With you, speaking formally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Con usted. And with you guys?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Con ustedes. The word for "for" is para. So how would you say "for him"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Para él, good. So when you decided that it was para él, you put para and con in the same group. And they are in the same group. They're in a group of words which are called prepositions.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now prepositions show some kind of movement or position, and they're very important and interesting words, so it's useful for us to identify them as we did with verbs and adjectives and nouns. So we're going to investigate now a little more about prepositions and how they behave in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, for him: para él. For her?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, para nosotras if it's an all-female group, good. Like I said, we don't say "for him" but "for he", and we don't say "for her" but "for she". With the exception of "me" and "you" informal, we get two different versions of the words for "me" and "you".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So "for me" is para mí, para mí. And "you" informal becomes ti. So "for you", speaking informally, is para ti. So this is just after prepositions we get this mí and ti, M-I and T-I.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we can find another preposition that we learned already. The word for "of" or "from". So again, this is a small word which is showing movement, direction, or position. These are prepositions. So, what was "of" or "from"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: De, good. So how would you say "from him"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, de mí, spelled M-I. And from you, speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Or ellas, good, de ellas. From us?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: De nosotros, good. From you guys?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Is it, is it from you guys?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Is it from you guys: ¿es de ustedes? How would you say "it's for you guys"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, es para ustedes, good. How would you say "it is with you guys"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now something to me doesn't feel right here. When we say es de ustedes ("it's from you guys") and es para ustedes ("it's for you guys"), we are speaking about things that are quite characteristic of whatever this thing is, whatever this "it" is. It's for you guys, it's from you guys.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But when we say "it's with you guys", we are speaking about a state because we are speaking about the location of something. So how do you think it will be "it is with you guys"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good, está con ustedes, very good. "To do" or "to make" was hacer, H-A-C-E-R.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hacer. So how would you say "he does" or "he's doing" or "he makes" or "he's making"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This is from haber, but well thought out, huh?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hace, good. "A favor" is un favor, un favor.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "he's doing me a favor", "he's doing me a favor"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Me hace un favor, good. How would you say "he's doing her a favor"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now if you say la hace, it sounds like he's making it, a feminine thing. If you want to say he's doing her a favor, for her, so what does la turn to to become "to her", "for her"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Le hace un favor, good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Decir is to tell. Now also we have hablar, to speak or to talk, and decir is to say or to tell, D-E-C-I-R. So decir in most of Spain, decir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how do you say "I want to tell", "I want to say"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I want, just think of "I want".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Quiero decir, huh? I want to tell him. I want to tell him.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. You have the option there of where you can put the le: before the changed verb or after the complete verb: le quiero decir, quiero decirle.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But if you want to say "I want to say it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo quiero decir. So we see actually with this le, we are kind of replacing a preposition with le and les, an imaginary preposition: "to", "for", "from".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, comprar. Comprar means to buy. I can say "I buy you something". Now this "you" is actually replacing "for you", "I buy something for you".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So what is "I buy" from comprar?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Compro. How do you say "I buy them" and you refer to the things that you're buying?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Los compro. But if you say "I buy them" and you mean "I buy for them"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Les compro. So this is the most natural Spanish structure: les compro. You use les instead of "for them", but you could say "I buy for them", you could do that if you wanted to using "for them" literally. So how would you say "I buy" or "I'm buying for them"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Compro para ellos. Good. So in an everyday situation "I'm buying something for them": les compro. Mostly we're going to be avoiding these prepositions. So, he buys it for me, I'm just going to say "he buys me it" rather than "he buys it for me". So how would you say that, "he buys me it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me lo compra. They buy me it or they buy it for me?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, me lo compran. They buy them for me, they buy them for me?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, me los compran, good. Now, we said that these small words: me, nos, te, le, les, most of the time what we are replacing with them is "to", but sometimes it's like "for", like to do a favor for, but they also might be replacing other prepositions like de.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, if I want to say "he buys it from me", I don't really need the "from" there either. I can just say "he buys me it". So how would I say that, "he buys it from me", "he buys me it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me lo compra. So this is totally ambiguous, no? It could mean "he buys it for me" or "he buys it from me", but it's something that we'll understand from the context.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So the key point to take away from here is that we probably use prepositions much more in English than in Spanish. And you just want to kind of like listen out for this and then you will start shedding them, you will start shedding your prepositions the more you listen to Spanish.
